claim: The docstring asserts each row is classified right only when the dialect arrives: with no dialect a data query naming another engine's catalog would be hidden, and a `#`-led SHOW would read as a data query and be shown.
source_excerpt:
Each row is classified right only when the dialect arrives: with no
    dialect, a data query naming another engine's catalog would be hidden
    too, and a ``#``-led ``SHOW`` would read as a data query and be shown.
verify_against: src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py is_introspection_query (None-dialect fallback union and SHOW detection)
verify_hint: Trace `is_introspection_query("# note\nSHOW TABLES", dialect=None)` and `is_introspection_query("SELECT id FROM sqlite_widgets", dialect=None)`; a None-dialect result of introspection for the first, or data for the second, falsifies it. Also note the first row's data query relies on the SQLite fallback-union entry (criterion 1/6).
evidence: Docstring at tests/unit/test_query_database.py:1164-1166. Row 1 (mysql URL, data_sql 'SELECT id FROM sqlite_widgets'): readonly.py _catalog_names (212-217) with dialect None returns _ALL_CATALOG_SCHEMAS/_ALL_CATALOG_NAME_PREFIXES, the union, which includes the sqlite entry ('sqlite_','pragma_') from _CATALOGS_BY_DIALECT (200-209); is_catalog_table (320-333) then does name.lower().startswith(prefixes) so 'sqlite_widgets' is a catalog table and is_introspection_query(dialect=None) returns True (hidden). Under dialect 'mysql', prefixes is () and schemas are only information_schema/mysql/sys/performance_schema, so it is data (shown). Row 2 ('# note\nSHOW TABLES'): under mysql, the MySQL tokenizer treats '#' as a line comment so first_sql_keyword returns 'SHOW' (254-293 returns True before parse). With None dialect, sqlglot's base Tokenizer has COMMENTS = ['--', ('/*','*/')] (sqlglot/tokens.py:563) and maps '#' to TokenType.HASH (tokens.py:156), so first_sql_keyword returns '' (non-word first token, readonly.py:160-163), the SHOW shortcut is skipped, and the text then either fails to parse (ParseError/TokenError caught, returns False at 296-303) or yields no catalog Table; in either case the result is False (data query, shown). I could not execute the code (no shell), so the None-dialect parse of the '#' text is traced from the tokenizer source, and the result is False on every branch. Both halves of the docstring hold. The other-engine-catalog row is the SQLite fallback-union entry, as the hint notes.

claim: The comment asserts that with lower_case_table_names = 0 MySQL looks a name up as written, and that the upper-case `_MYSQL_KINDS` rows therefore pin what the guard does with the type the catalog reports rather than how MySQL resolves letter case; this holds only if the fake reports lower_case_table_names = 0 and verify_base_tables passes the name as written.
source_excerpt:
# The objects of ``database`` as a MySQL server reports them. The upper-case
# names are separate entries: with lower_case_table_names = 0, MySQL looks a
# name up as written, so these rows pin what the guard does with the type the
# catalog reports, not how MySQL resolves letter case.
verify_against: tests/unit/_fake_pymysql.py (the @@lower_case_table_names answer) and src/sqllens/safety/relations.py (identifier-case policy handling for mode 0)
verify_hint: Check what FakeMySQL returns for `SELECT @@lower_case_table_names` and how `verify_base_tables` in `relations.py` normalizes the looked-up table name under each mode, in particular mode 0.
evidence: Both conditions hold. (1) tests/unit/_fake_pymysql.py:152 defaults FakeMySQL.lower_case_table_names to 0, and _CatalogCursor.execute (line 73-74) answers the parameterless `SELECT @@lower_case_table_names` with (server.lower_case_table_names,). _mysql_server in test_rls_views.py:72-75 builds FakeMySQL(kinds=...) with **kwargs and no override at the comment's call sites, so mode 0 applies. (2) src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:147-153 sets mysql_fold = mode[0] != 0, so mode 0 gives no LOWER() wrapping (168-170). The name is passed as written: _relations (51-70) uses sqlglot.parse_one with no normalization or lower-casing, and line 175 passes relation.name as the %s argument. The fake looks it up with `params[1] in server.kinds` (_fake_pymysql.py:75-76), an exact-case dict lookup, so ORDERS and orders are separate entries. That matches the comment: under mode 0 the upper-case rows pin how the guard handles the reported TABLE_TYPE, and the fake does no letter-case resolution of its own. Real MySQL with lower_case_table_names=0 compares names case-sensitively, and the guard uses BINARY comparison.
